messages.subject: Breaking up words into syllables
parts:
Dear All,

I'm interested in the relationship of the frequency of a word and its
length measured in syllables. Here's three questions related to this
topic:

1. Does anyone know of an R function to break up words into syllables
and/or to count syllables in words?
2. What could be elements for a script to break up words into
syllables/count syllables in words?
3. Is anyone aware of published work on the relationship, perhaps
(negative) correlation, of word frequency and word length?

Thanks in advance

Chris

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Breaking up words into syllables
parts:
Dear Chris,

I would strongly suggest against doing this yourself. At least for English (and probably most languages), breaking words into syllables is a hard NLP task. I would recommend you use a dictionary with syllable information where you can look up the word and see how many syllables it has.

Best,

MGN

messages.author: 3957c1a92561c3c1
messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Breaking up words into syllables
parts:
Dear Chris,

I had a similar issue and wrote a little code snippet which counts the number of syllables of words in a string - it was sufficient for my purpose but is neigther very neat nor sophisticated. feel free to improve on it. CAUTION the code is horrible!

best,
martin

here is the code:

# syl.len is s function which counts the number of syllables of words
# syl.len takes one argument: a vector of words and returns a matrix with the
# number of syllables in the first and only column. the column has the same number
# of rows as the input vector.
syl.len <- function(x) {
  require(stringr)                    # activate
  x <- str_split(x, " ")              # split up all words into individual letters
  sapply(x, function(y){
    syl <- tolower(y)                   # convert all characters to lower case
    syl <- gsub("[A|a]o", "aco", syl)   # chaos  (would be recognized as monosyllabic if this line is not included
    syl <- gsub("e$", "", syl)          # remove word final e: usually not nucleus
    syl <- gsub("ei", "e", syl)         # collapse diphthongs
    syl <- gsub("ue", "u", syl)         # collapse diphthongs
    syl <- gsub("io", "i", syl)         # collapse diphthongs
    syl <- gsub("ie", "i", syl)         # collapse diphthongs
    syl <- gsub("oo", "o", syl)         # collapse diphthongs
    syl <- gsub("ee", "e", syl)         # collapse diphthongs
    syl <- gsub("-", "", syl)           # remove en dashes in compounds
    syl <- str_trim(syl, side = "both") # remove superfluous spaces
    syllex <- gsub("[b|c|d|f|g|h|j|k|l|m|n|p|q|r|s|t|v|w|x|z]", "", syl) # remove consonants
    syllex <- gsub(" ", "", syllex)     # remove superfluous spaces
    syl <- nchar(syllex)                # count number of nuclei
    result <- as.vector(unlist(syl))
    } )
  }

# test
test <- c("this is just a test question")
syl.len(test)

If possible, you can use the CELEX database, which will cover a lot of
word types and is easily processable with R. (You can also use that to
check how well Martin's script is doing.)
